title: Bangladesh garment unrest flares again as wage board talks stall; factories shut near Dhaka
dek: Workers blocked the Dhaka-Mymensingh highway for a second day and Gazipur factories sent staff home for a fifth day; the wage board, whose last meeting was postponed, meets on 23 November.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Garment factories around Dhaka stayed shut on Thursday for a fifth straight day in parts of Gazipur as a fresh wave of protests over the minimum wage spread across Bangladesh's main export hubs, with workers blocking the Dhaka-Mymensingh highway again and police using tear gas and sound grenades to disperse them, according to reports. Workers want the monthly minimum raised to Tk 30,000 from Tk 12,500, a rise of 140 per cent.

The new round of unrest began on Monday after a meeting of the government's Minimum Wage Board was postponed when a member representing workers said he was unwell, according to reports citing the manufacturers' association BGMEA. The board says it will next meet on 23 November. About 500 of the country's roughly 4,500 garment factories were shut at one point this week, one report said, citing unnamed sources.

## What happened this week

On Wednesday police in Savar, outside Dhaka, used tear gas, stun grenades and batons after protesters blocked a highway and, according to the local police chief, Saiful Alam, "threw stones at them", reports said. In Ashulia about 25 factories closed, and in Gazipur protesters blocked the Dhaka-Mymensingh highway and set fire to a police vehicle. No count of injuries has been published.

On Thursday workers in Gazipur reported for their shifts and were again sent home shortly after arriving, one report said. Gazipur's industrial police chief, Amjad Hossain, confirmed that 10 factories had declared a general holiday for the day. Between 400 and 500 workers blocked the Dhaka-Mymensingh highway at Natun Bazar in Sreepur at about 10.30 am (10 am IST) before police dispersed them, and workers alleged that police fired sound grenades at them as they left the factories, reports said.

Many factories have stayed shut under the "no work, no pay" provision of the Bangladesh Labour Act, which lets owners suspend operations during unrest. The BGMEA and the knitwear makers' association BKMEA have asked for protection for factories and called in a joint statement for wage talks to resume as soon as possible. Border Guard Bangladesh said its headquarters was "closely observing the situation from a monitoring cell" and had stepped up patrols using drones and body-worn cameras.

"The owners seem unwilling to meet our salary demands. They are already dragging their feet," one worker in Gazipur told reporters.

## Background

The government of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman set up the wage board earlier this month after an earlier wave of protests that disrupted more than 500 factories. At its first meeting, the board agreed that a new minimum wage would take effect in December and show in January pay, but it has not agreed an amount. The current minimum was set in December 2023 after protests that year. The industry earns about $40 billion a year from exports, employs about four million people, most of them women from rural areas, and is entering its busiest season ahead of Christmas orders.

## Why it matters for India and Bengal

India's garment exporters compete with Bangladesh for orders from the same global brands, and a long disruption could push some buyers to shift orders around the region. Bangladesh's factories also depend on cotton, yarn and fabric from India, much of it carried by road through West Bengal's Petrapole-Benapole crossing, so prolonged closures hurt traders and transporters on the Indian side as well.

## What happens next

The wage board meets on 23 November. The new minimum wage is expected to be announced in December and to take effect in January, once it is gazetted.
